sections.facts: The Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, came into operation in the city of Poona on February 15, 1950. Section 127(2) authorized the Corporation to impose octroi and other taxes, and Section 149 prescribed the procedure for levying taxes. In 1957, the Corporation decided to offer concessions, including exemption from octroi duty, to encourage industrial development. Rule 62B was introduced, defining an 'Industrial Estate or Area' as an area the Corporation might demarcate for industries to be suitably located in the interest of Poona's industrialization. Under this rule, no octroi was to be levied for twelve years. Later, new octroi rules were framed in 1962, with Rule 5(8) providing for octroi exemption. The Corporation levied octroi on materials received by the appellants, who sought exemption under Rule 5(8). The Corporation denied the exemption, stating it could only be granted if the area was declared and demarcated as an industrial area. Aggrieved, the appellants filed writ petitions under Article 226 of the Constitution, seeking a mandamus to compel the Corporation to define and demarcate their factory areas as industrial areas under Rule 5(8) and exempt them from octroi. During the pendency of these petitions, Rule 5(8) was repealed. The appellants amended their petitions, arguing that the repeal was illegal and that they were still entitled to the benefit of the unrepealed Rule 62B. The High Court rejected both contentions, holding that both old Rule 62B and new Rule 5(8) were repealed without legal flaw. The High Court also found that the area in question was not demarcated as an industrial estate or area for the purpose of Rule 5(8) and that demarcation was solely at the Corporation's discretion. Consequently, the writ petitions were dismissed.
sections.statute: The Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, Section 127(2) authorized the Corporation to impose octroi and other taxes. Section 149 prescribed the procedure for levying taxes. Rule 62B, introduced in 1957, defined 'Industrial Estate or Area' and provided for a twelve-year exemption from octroi. New octroi rules were framed in 1962, with Rule 5(8) providing for exemption. The preamble to the new octroi Rules indicated the rescission of certain rules, including those related to octroi, and the enactment of new rules. Rule 5(8) was later repealed by a notification effective September 1, 1968, with a proviso that exemptions already granted would continue until their expiry.
sections.argument: On appeal, the appellants contended that the disputed area had been included in the development plan under the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, before Rule 5(8) was promulgated, thus automatically becoming an industrial estate or area for the purposes of that rule. They also argued that the Corporation arbitrarily refused exemption because their concerns were not new. Furthermore, they claimed a violation of Article 14 of the Constitution, asserting that some industries in similar situations had received exemptions while they were denied the benefit of Rule 5(8). Finally, they argued that the Corporation considered extraneous or irrelevant factors when denying the exemption. For the respondent, it was contended that Rule 5(8) had been deleted, precluding exemption under it. The appellants' reply was that they could still rely on the old Rule 62B, as it had not been repealed, and that the repeal of Rule 5(8) was illegal. They also relied on the proviso to the repealing resolution.
sections.analysis: The Court found that no area had been declared an industrial area under the Development Plan before 1957; the disputed area only became an industrial area under the Bombay Town Planning Act after the enforcement of the development plan on August 15, 1966. A perusal of Rule 5(8) indicated that for octroi exemption, an industrial estate or area meant an area demarcated by the Corporation specifically for that rule's purpose, to encourage industrialization. Therefore, a demarcation under the Town Planning Act was not a demarcation for the purpose of Rule 5(8), and without such demarcation, exemption could not be claimed. The Court agreed with the High Court's view based on Rule 5(8). The purpose of the Town Planning Act is town planning, separating industrial areas from residential or commercial zones, whereas the purpose of demarcation under Rule 5(8) is to provide incentives for industries. The Court analyzed the preamble to the new octroi Rules and concluded that Rule 62B was repealed by implication, as the new comprehensive rules covered the same subject matter, including exemption for industrial areas, and it was unlikely the rule-making authority intended to have two rules on the same subject. The Court noted that the proviso to the repealing resolution, stating that already granted exemptions would continue, did not benefit the appellants as they had never been granted an exemption under Rule 5(8). The considerations that led the Corporation to deny exemption were deemed relevant and within the ambit of Rule 5(8). The Court found no foundation for the claim of Article 14 violation, as it was not alleged or proven that any other unit received exemption without the Corporation's demarcation under Rule 5(8).
sections.judgement: The appeals were dismissed. The Court held that the demarcation under the Town Planning Act was not equivalent to the demarcation required by Rule 5(8) for octroi exemption. It was also held that Rule 62B was repealed by implication by the new comprehensive octroi rules, including Rule 5(8). The proviso to the repealing resolution did not apply as the appellants had not been granted prior exemption. The considerations used by the Corporation were found to be relevant and within the scope of Rule 5(8). The contention of Article 14 violation was rejected due to lack of evidence. The appeals were dismissed, with parties bearing their own costs.
